title: Future work: applying Transformer to other tasks
description: The authors plan to apply the Transformer to a broader range of tasks beyond machine translation and constituency parsing.
canonical_description: applying architecture to broader range of tasks

evidence.anchor: plan to apply them to other tasks
evidence.quote: We are excited about the future of attention-based models and plan to apply them to other tasks.

evidence.anchor: extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text
evidence.quote: We plan to extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text and to investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video.

verdict.reasoning: The gap asked whether Transformers could be applied to a broader range of tasks beyond machine translation and constituency parsing. Five papers in five distinct domains (music generation, engineering physics / PDE solving, online gesture recognition of mathematical expressions, medical image diagnosis with clinical records, and robotic learning from demonstrations) each demonstrate successful Transformer applications — four as direct_solution, one as partial_solution. Collectively, they show the architecture generalizes across creative, scientific, HCI, medical, and robotic domains, with concrete empirical results. No meaningful piece of the original question remains open: Transformers clearly can be applied to and work well on a broad range of tasks. High confidence because the evidence spans multiple independent papers with strong results across diverse domains.

paper.title: Music Transformer
paper.abstract: Music relies heavily on repetition to build structure and meaning. Self-reference occurs on multiple timescales, from motifs to phrases to reusing of entire sections of music, such as in pieces with ABA structure. The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), a sequence model based on self-attention, has achieved compelling results in many generation tasks that require maintaining long-range coherence. This suggests that self-attention might also be well-suited to modeling music. In musical composition and performance, however, relative timing is critically important. Existing approaches for representing relative positional information in the Transformer modulate attention based on pairwise distance (Shaw et al., 2018). This is impractical for long sequences such as musical compositions since their memory complexity for intermediate relative information is quadratic in the sequence length. We propose an algorithm that reduces their intermediate memory requirement to linear in the sequence length. This enables us to demonstrate that a Transformer with our modified relative attention mechanism can generate minute-long compositions (thousands of steps, four times the length modeled in Oore et al., 2018) with compelling structure, generate continuations that coherently elaborate on a given motif, and in a seq2seq setup generate accompaniments conditioned on melodies. We evaluate the Transformer with our relative attention mechanism on two datasets, JSB Chorales and Piano-e-Competition, and obtain state-of-the-art results on the latter.

assessments.contribution_summary: The Music Transformer paper applies the Transformer architecture — originally designed for machine translation and constituency parsing — to the task of symbolic music generation. It demonstrates that a Transformer with a modified relative attention mechanism can generate minute-long musical compositions with long-term structure, generate continuations that elaborate on given motifs, and produce accompaniments conditioned on melodies. The paper evaluates on two music datasets (JSB Chorales and Piano-e-Competition) and achieves state-of-the-art results on the latter, showing that Transformers can be successfully applied to a creative, structured domain far beyond their original NLP tasks.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap of applying Transformers to a broader range of tasks beyond machine translation and constituency parsing — specifically, it applies Transformers to music generation. However, the gap as stated ("applying Transformer to other tasks") is broad; this paper covers one new task (music generation) but does not address other potential tasks such as image generation, video, speech, code generation, scientific modeling, or other domains. The gap of applying Transformers to those other tasks remains open.
evidence_snippets: Domain contributions\hspace{1em} We show the first successful use of Transformers in generating music that exhibits long-term structure.
In this work we demonstrated that the Transformer equipped with relative attention is very well-suited for generative modeling of symbolic music.

Our memory-efficient implementation enables the application of relative attention to much longer sequences such as long texts or even audio waveforms, which significantly broadens the range of problems to which it could be applied.

paper.title: Beyond Language: Applying MLX Transformers to Engineering Physics
paper.abstract: Transformer Neural Networks are driving an explosion of activity and discovery in the field of Large Language Models (LLMs). In contrast, there have been only a few attempts to apply Transformers in engineering physics. Aiming to offer an easy entry point to physics-centric Transformers, we introduce a physics-informed Transformer model for solving the heat conduction problem in a 2D plate with Dirichlet boundary conditions. The model is implemented in the machine learning framework MLX and leverages the unified memory of Apple M-series processors. The use of MLX means that the models can be trained and perform predictions efficiently on personal machines with only modest memory requirements. To train, validate and test the Transformer model we solve the 2D heat conduction problem using central finite differences. Each finite difference solution in these sets is initialized with four random Dirichlet boundary conditions, a uniform but random internal temperature distribution and a randomly selected thermal diffusivity. Validation is performed in-line during training to monitor against over-fitting. The excellent performance of the trained model is demonstrated by predicting the evolution of the temperature field to steady state for the unseen test set of conditions.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper applies a standard Transformer architecture (without ad-hoc physics modifications) to solve the 2D heat conduction problem with Dirichlet boundary conditions, implemented in the MLX framework. It demonstrates that pure Transformer models can learn differential operators and predict temperature field evolution, achieving excellent performance in both block prediction and autoregressive inference modes. The paper serves as a tutorial/introduction aimed at engineers, drawing analogies between Transformer mechanisms (self-attention, positional embeddings) and familiar engineering concepts (Fourier transforms, wavelets, cross-correlation).
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap calls for applying Transformers to a "broader range of tasks" — this paper only addresses a single task (2D heat conduction). It does not demonstrate generalization across multiple diverse engineering/physics tasks, nor does it explore other types of PDEs (e.g., Navier-Stokes, wave equation, elasticity), other physics domains (fluid dynamics, structural mechanics, electromagnetics), or non-PDE engineering tasks. The paper itself acknowledges this limitation, listing as future work: scalability to more complex boundary conditions, higher-dimensional PDEs, larger grids, and comparison to other architectures. The broader range of tasks beyond the single heat conduction problem remains unaddressed.
evidence_snippets: This paper, therefore, addresses the research question of whether standard Transformer architectures are capable of `learning' differential operators by themselves, without the support of ad-hoc solutions. To provide a friendly introduction to these physics-centric Transformers, we train a Transformer model to predict the solutions of heat conduction in a 2D plate with Dirichlet boundary conditions (BCs).

With the potential of Transformers established, we next plan to explore the performance of this class of NNs in more challenging applications. In particular, we are working on implementing Transformer-augmented subgrid models for use with Large Eddy Simulations of turbulent fluid flows.

Future work will involve testing the model's ability to generalize to more complex boundary conditions, higher-dimensional PDEs, and larger grids. This includes assessing the model's behavior when scaling up both spatial resolution and temporal duration.

paper.title: A Transformer Architecture for Online Gesture Recognition of Mathematical Expressions
paper.abstract: The Transformer architecture is shown to provide a powerful framework as an end-to-end model for building expression trees from online handwritten gestures corresponding to glyph strokes. In particular, the attention mechanism was successfully used to encode, learn and enforce the underlying syntax of expressions creating latent representations that are correctly decoded to the exact mathematical expression tree, providing robustness to ablated inputs and unseen glyphs. For the first time, the encoder is fed with spatio-temporal data tokens potentially forming an infinitely large vocabulary, which finds applications beyond that of online gesture recognition. A new supervised dataset of online handwriting gestures is provided for training models on generic handwriting recognition tasks and a new metric is proposed for the evaluation of the syntactic correctness of the output expression trees. A small Transformer model suitable for edge inference was successfully trained to an average normalised Levenshtein accuracy of 94%, resulting in valid postfix RPN tree representation for 94% of predictions.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper applies the Transformer architecture to online gesture recognition of mathematical expressions — a task fundamentally different from machine translation and constituency parsing. It modifies the Transformer encoder to accept spatio-temporal stroke data as real-valued tokens (rather than discrete vocabulary embeddings), and uses the decoder to generate expression trees in Reverse Polish Notation. The paper demonstrates that Transformers can handle multi-level segmentation (glyph and numeral), learn syntactic/semantic rules implicitly, and exhibit transfer learning from a completely different domain (language modeling) to this new task.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap of applying Transformers to a new task beyond machine translation and constituency parsing. It demonstrates a successful application to online gesture recognition of mathematical expressions. However, the gap calls for applying Transformers to a "broader range of tasks" in general, and this paper only covers one specific new task (mathematical expression tree building from gestures). Other tasks beyond this specific domain remain unexplored.
evidence_snippets: For the first time, the encoder is fed with spatio-temporal data tokens potentially forming an infinitely large vocabulary, which finds applications beyond that of online gesture recognition.

We prove the power of Transformers not only as language models but also as a solution to several sequence mapping tasks, demonstrating transfer learning behaviours of the encoder on unseen glyphs from online gesture input
Neural Machine Translation may be extended in this way to online data at different granularity levels, with no need for separate input segmentation or complex positional embeddings.

paper.title: Transformer-based Personalized Attention Mechanism for Medical Images with Clinical Records
paper.abstract: In medical image diagnosis, identifying the attention region, i.e., the region of interest for which the diagnosis is made, is an important task. Various methods have been developed to automatically identify target regions from given medical images. However, in actual medical practice, the diagnosis is made based not only on the images but also on a variety of clinical records. This means that pathologists examine medical images with some prior knowledge of the patients and that the attention regions may change depending on the clinical records. In this study, we propose a method called the Personalized Attention Mechanism (PersAM), by which the attention regions in medical images are adaptively changed according to the clinical records. The primary idea of the PersAM method is to encode the relationships between the medical images and clinical records using a variant of Transformer architecture. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the PersAM method, we applied it to a large-scale digital pathology problem of identifying the subtypes of 842 malignant lymphoma patients based on their gigapixel whole slide images and clinical records.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper applies a Transformer-based architecture (PersAM) to a multimodal medical diagnosis task — specifically, subtype classification of malignant lymphoma using whole slide images and clinical records. The Transformer encodes relationships between image patches, clinical factors, and class tokens to produce personalized attention regions. This directly addresses the gap of applying Transformers beyond machine translation and constituency parsing, demonstrating their use in medical image analysis with multimodal inputs.
assessments.what_remains_open: This paper fully addresses the gap for the specific case of applying Transformers to medical image diagnosis with clinical records. However, the gap as stated ("applying Transformer to other tasks") is broad and open-ended — this paper solves it for one particular task domain (digital pathology), but the gap of applying Transformers to *all* other possible tasks beyond translation and parsing remains open by its nature. The paper itself acknowledges this by focusing on a specific application (malignant lymphoma) while noting the framework could be applied to other similar problem settings.
evidence_snippets: The proposed PersAM method employs a variant of the Transformer architecture to encode the relationships between the medical images and corresponding clinical records.
The application of Transformer architecture to computer vision can calculate attention regions calculated by encoding the relationship between image patches.

In this study, we introduce a framework, called the Personalized Attention Mechanism (PersAM) framework, that adaptively changes the attention regions in medical images according to patient-specific information.

paper.title: Transformer-XL for Long Sequence Tasks in Robotic Learning from Demonstration
paper.abstract: This paper presents an innovative application of Transformer-XL for long sequence tasks in robotic learning from demonstrations (LfD). The proposed framework effectively integrates multi-modal sensor inputs, including RGB-D images, LiDAR, and tactile sensors, to construct a comprehensive feature vector. By leveraging the advanced capabilities of Transformer-XL, particularly its attention mechanism and position encoding, our approach can handle the inherent complexities and long-term dependencies of multi-modal sensory data. The results of an extensive empirical evaluation demonstrate significant improvements in task success rates, accuracy, and computational efficiency compared to conventional methods such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The findings indicate that the Transformer-XL-based framework not only enhances the robot's perception and decision-making abilities but also provides a robust foundation for future advancements in robotic learning from demonstrations.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper applies Transformer-XL (a Transformer variant) to robotic learning from demonstrations (LfD), which is a task domain far beyond the original Transformer applications of machine translation and constituency parsing. The paper presents a complete framework integrating multi-modal sensor inputs (RGB-D, LiDAR, tactile) with Transformer-XL encoding, trained via behavior cloning and PPO on the RoboMimic dataset, with empirical results showing improvements over LSTM and CNN baselines.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap is fully addressed by this paper — it demonstrates a concrete application of a Transformer architecture to a new task domain (robotic LfD) beyond the originally mentioned tasks. The paper does not claim to exhaust all possible tasks, but it directly fulfills the stated future work of applying Transformers to other tasks.
evidence_snippets: This paper presents an innovative application of Transformer-XL for long sequence tasks in robotic learning from demonstrations (LfD).
We have successfully applied Transformer-XL to robotic learning and demonstrated its ability to perform long sequence tasks and navigate the complex dependencies inherent in multimodal sensory input.

The Transformer architecture, with its attention mechanism, can handle long-term dependencies much better than traditional recurrent neural networks... This has revolutionized natural language processing, and this success has sparked a strong interest in exploring applications of Transformer in other domains, including robotics.
